title: How Animal Domestication Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore animal domestication, starting with Jared Diamond's ideas that animal domestication and the Neolithic agricultural revolution changed humans, and that humans themselves became "domesticated." They define domestication (genetically altered species that can no longer feed themselves, born comfortable around humans) versus tameness and feralness, discuss cats as an exception, and cover artificial selection in horses, sheep, chickens and dogs. Diamond's six-point checklist for domesticable animals is covered, along with the history of dog domestication, the Russian silver fox experiment by Dmitri Belyaev, and the domestication of cattle, camels, goats, pigs, oxen, donkeys, horses, turkeys, and bees. They close with how agriculture led to human changes and epidemic diseases from livestock, then a listener mail segment about Nielsen TV ratings families.
topics: domesticated vs tamed vs feral animals

segments.title: Opening banter and Jared Diamond's agriculture argument
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and Jared Diamond's article arguing that domestication of animals and agriculture changed Homo sapiens, and that humans became domesticated too. They joke about aliens seeing an animal riding an animal.

segments.title: Definitions: domesticated, tame, and feral animals
segments.summary: A domesticated animal is a formerly wild species whose genetics were altered by humans so it can no longer feed itself and is born comfortable with humans. Tame wolves and feral animals are contrasted, and cats are discussed as an exception.
topics: domesticated vs tamed vs feral animals

segments.title: Artificial selection in horses, sheep, chickens and dogs
segments.summary: Artificial selection by breeding for size, wool, and egg-laying is described, including horses bred bigger, sheep bred for wool over kemp, and chickens, with the first chickens possibly domesticated for cockfighting.

segments.title: Criteria for domestication and Diamond's checklist
segments.summary: Diamond found only about fourteen of 148 candidate species were domesticated. The hosts walk through the criteria: diet, fast growth, friendly disposition, easy breeding, social hierarchy, and not panicking. Examples include koalas, zebras, and grizzlies.

segments.title: Squarespace sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace website builder with a free trial and offer code.

segments.title: History of domestication and the Fertile Crescent region animals
segments.summary: Dogs were likely the first domesticated animal, long before agriculture. Around 10,500 years ago climate change and megafauna loss led to agriculture and the domestication of pigs, sheep and cattle. Regional origins of animals are listed across Asia, Arabia, Ukraine, Egypt and South America.

segments.title: Dogs, tameness, and the Belyaev silver fox experiment
segments.summary: Hosts distinguish domesticated animals from tamed ones such as hamsters and wolves. They describe Dmitri Belyaev's silver fox experiment, in which foxes developed floppy ears, smaller skulls, curly hair, barking, and friendliness. Dogs' early history with hunter-gatherers is covered, along with theories of how dogs began.

segments.title: Cats, working animals, and livestock spread
segments.summary: Cats are discussed as probably not fully domesticated, descended from European and African wildcats, with an early grave evidence. Cattle, oxen, goats, pigs, donkeys, and camels are covered for milk, work, wool, and transport. Domestication helped spread agriculture along trade routes.

segments.title: Turkeys, bees, and humans becoming domesticated
segments.summary: Turkeys were domesticated by Mesoamericans, and bees were domesticated with L.L. Langstroth's movable frames in 1852. The hosts discuss whether bees, silkworms, rabbits and hamsters count as domesticated. They close with how agriculture changed humans and spread epidemic diseases from livestock.

segments.title: Nielsen TV ratings family listener mail
segments.summary: A listener email from an Atlanta family in the Nielsen ratings panel describes having TV and computer usage tracked for pay and being a 'Grand Slam' family.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to social media and email for contact.
